scenarios.name: Baseline
scenarios.assumptions: The selected model's own dynamics; no shift.

scenarios.name: Accelerated China pull
scenarios.assumptions: Chinese demand and finance keep growing: the yearly change in the export share to China is 2 points above the model's, the share to the United States 1 point below; the index moves 2 points a year toward China and 1 away from the United States.

scenarios.name: US sourcing rules bite
scenarios.assumptions: IRA-style sourcing rules, the Minerals Security Partnership and tariffs divert flows: the yearly change in the export share to the United States is 2 points above the model's, the share to China 2 points below; the index moves 2 points a year each way.

components.name: trade_export_share
components.definition: Share of the country's mineral exports (reported to UN Comtrade) that go to the actor.

components.name: trade_import_share
components.definition: Share of the country's mineral imports that come from the actor.

components.name: finance_flow
components.definition: Documented official-finance commitments from the actor's institutions over the last three years, relative to GDP; central-bank swap-line drawdowns excluded.

components.name: debt_stock
components.definition: Public and publicly guaranteed external debt owed to the actor, relative to GDP (World Bank IDS reports China as a creditor; no equivalent source exists for the United States).

components.name: diplomatic_alignment
components.definition: UN General Assembly voting agreement with the actor in the year.

components.name: legislative_stance
components.definition: Mean stance toward the actor (−2 to +2) in the legislature's mineral-related records, years with at least five scored records; a text-model output carried with its validation status.

index_rules.formula: normalised = clip(raw, lo, hi) − lo over hi − lo, times 100; index = mean of the available normalised components (at least three)

findings.title: Who talks, who pays
findings.headline: Washington out-talks Beijing 1.8 to 1; Beijing out-lends Washington 11.8 to 1

sentences.text: United States officials account for 70 of the 417 statements in the dataset and Chinese officials for 39; 42 of the 46 US statements that take a position on China are negative, while 37 of the 37 Chinese statements with a position praise China's role.

The money runs the other way: documented commitments from Chinese institutions to the 20 countries reached US$77.1 bn in 2015–2021 (US$13.0 bn of it tagged to a mineral by the adapters), US DFC and EXIM commitments US$6.5 bn in the same years and US$3.5 bn in 2022–2024.
That is 1.8 US statements for every Chinese one, and 11.8 Chinese dollars committed for every American one over 2015–2021.

strength.basis: statement counts from the owner's dataset (dozens per bloc) against documented commitments; both finance sources record every sector

findings.caveat: AidData ends in 2021 and US finance comes from the DFC and EXIM, so the comparison runs on the years both sides cover; the statements were gathered by web search, which favours prominent US voices.

findings.title: Argentina: words and trade
findings.headline: Argentina: warm to Washington, 0.2% of exports; warm to Beijing, 23% of exports

strength.basis: 5 coded executive statements at the thinnest point against reported exports; the stance coding is the dataset's own and not validated

findings.caveat: A warm word costs nothing and a trade share moves slowly; the two can differ for years without anyone being insincere.

Peru: China took 48% of mineral exports in 2024; the 2030 medians are 61% at baseline, 73% if the China pull accelerates and 49% if US sourcing rules bite; the US share 5.6% at baseline and 18% under reshoring.

Brazil: China took 48% of mineral exports in 2025; the 2030 medians are 56% at baseline, 66% if the China pull accelerates and 46% if US sourcing rules bite; the US share 2.6% at baseline and 13% under reshoring.

Chile: China took 48% of mineral exports in 2025; the 2030 medians are 56% at baseline, 66% if the China pull accelerates and 46% if US sourcing rules bite; the US share 14% at baseline and 24% under reshoring.

strength.basis: backtested models (persistence where nothing beat it; backtest origins 2007–2023, 2007–2024) with scenarios as stated yearly shifts

findings.caveat: Five-year paths from annual series of at most 26 points (2000–2025) carry wide bands; the scenarios are what-ifs with stated assumptions, not predictions.

findings.title: After the shock
findings.headline: What followed US tariff measures: +4.5 points for China's share within two years

sentences.text: After US tariff measures (19 event-country windows from 1 event, all still in draft), the share of exports to China moved +4.5 points on average within two years (middle half +0.0 points to +8.9 points).

After US strategy measures (38 event-country windows from 2 events, all still in draft), the share of exports to China moved +3.6 points on average within two years (middle half +0.0 points to +6.0 points).

After Chinese export control measures (66 event-country windows from 4 events, all still in draft), the share of exports to China moved +1.4 points on average within two years (middle half -2.1 points to +1.9 points).

strength.basis: event windows on annual shares with placebo distributions; the event list is still in draft

findings.caveat: Windows overlap, events cluster in the same years and world prices move everything at once: these are echoes, not effects.

findings.title: What the panel says
findings.headline: Chinese money does not buy export share; democracy buys American imports

sentences.text: Across the panel (19 countries, 2002–2021), Chinese commitments over the previous three years go with a change of +0.5 points in the share of exports to China the next year per standard deviation (wild-cluster p 0.70; dropping one country at a time keeps it between -0.5 points and +2.3 points): the money is not followed by more mineral trade, if anything by slightly less.

The one robust political association runs through imports: a country one standard deviation more democratic (about 0.17 on the 0–1 V-Dem index, Nicaragua 2021 to Uruguay 2012 being 0.72 apart) buys 1.5 points more of its mineral imports from the United States (wild-cluster p 0.82; -2.8 points to +5.2 points dropping one country at a time).

strength.basis: two-way fixed-effects panel with cluster-robust and wild-bootstrap inference and leave-one-country-out ranges; associations only

findings.caveat: 19 clusters and 20 years (2002–2021): a single country can move a coefficient, and year effects absorb the price swings that drive most of the variation.

human.title: Reading the contrasts: what the words, the money and the minerals say together
human.author: AI-drafted from the site's indicators; not yet reviewed by the project owner
human.text_md:
## How to read this

This text was drafted from the indicators on this page, not from outside knowledge. Every claim names in square brackets the finding or indicator it rests on; the numbers quoted are the ones the page shows for the data release named above and they change with each release. It is an interpretation, bolder than the generated findings, and the project owner has not yet reviewed it. Treat it as a reading to argue with, not a result.

## What the contrasts show

The loudest voice is not the biggest spender [who_talks_who_pays]. US officials produce 1.8 statements on South American minerals for every Chinese one, and more than nine in ten of their coded positions on China are hostile; Chinese officials speak less and only in praise of their own role. Over the seven years both finance records cover, Chinese institutions committed about twenty times more money to the twelve countries than the DFC and EXIM did. This asymmetry is the central fact of the page: Washington argues, Beijing lends. The caveat matters: the Chinese figures include ports, power and budget support, and only about a sixth of the money is tagged to a mineral [talk_vs_money]. Even so, the mineral-tagged part alone exceeds the whole US record.

Warm words travel in one direction and the ore in the other [words_vs_trade_ARG, words_vs_trade_PER, words_vs_trade_BOL]. The executives of Argentina, Peru and Bolivia are almost uniformly positive about the United States in their coded statements of 2024–2026, while the United States takes a few per cent of their mineral exports and China a quarter to a half. Brazil and Chile are cooler in tone toward both powers and trade the most with China [words_vs_trade_BRA, words_vs_trade_CHL]. The reading: rhetoric toward Washington is a diplomatic register, not a trade signal. Where words and shares diverge most, the words are the cheaper of the two.

Leaders talk about the minerals they do not yet sell [talk_vs_trade_ARG, talk_vs_trade_BOL, talk_vs_trade_BRA, talk_vs_trade_CHL]. Lithium takes most of the mineral mentions in Argentina, Bolivia and Chile and rare earths in Brazil; the export value comes from gold, silver, copper and iron ore. The mismatch is largest where the promised mineral is least exported. This is not hypocrisy: politicians speak about what is contested and new. But it means the statements dataset measures aspiration while trade measures the past, and the two should never be read as the same thing.

Hedging is the regional posture, not the exception [hedging]. Argentina, Bolivia and Peru praise both powers and their executives record no coded negative toward China at all. Brazil stands apart with coded negatives toward the United States [words_vs_trade_BRA]. In a region where China buys and the United States talks, praising both costs nothing and keeps the option to sell to either.

The money did not move the minerals [money_without_trade, panel]. Eight large commitments, all Chinese and mostly outside mining, were followed by no shift in where the receiving country's minerals went. The panel regression says the same in general form: Chinese lending over the previous three years goes with a slightly lower, not higher, share of exports to China the next year, and the association is indistinguishable from zero. The simplest reading is that Chinese finance in this region bought infrastructure and goodwill while the ore followed prices and geology. Influence and dependence are kept in different ledgers.

Parliaments are mostly silent on the China question [parliament_vs_executive, cannot_see]. The legislatures' coded records take a position on China in a dozen or two documents a year, and where they do (Argentina and Brazil in 2026) they sound no cooler than the executives. The contest that US statements describe does not appear as a domestic legislative argument. Either the matter is settled between executives and companies, or the records do not capture it; both readings fit the data.

Attention without money [attention]. US policy documents on minerals in the warehouse grew five-fold since 2000, from 24 documents to 122 in 2025 (181 so far in 2026), while DFC and EXIM commitments to the twelve countries peaked at US$1.1 bn in 2022 and fell to US$24 m so far in 2026. The gap between the paper trail and the cheque is the US side of the first contrast.

## Future perspective to 2030

The published models expect persistence [fork_2030]. Under the baseline, China's share of mineral exports stays above half in Peru, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador and rises where the trend already points up (Peru, Ecuador). The scenario in which US sourcing rules bite, a shift of two points a year for five years, still leaves China with more than two fifths of those countries' exports; the United States reaches about a quarter in Chile and a third in Colombia, where it is already the larger buyer. The arithmetic of parity makes the same point [parity]: for the United States to buy as much as China does in Chile, Brazil or Peru, about ten billion dollars of yearly exports would have to change hands in each, several times what it buys today. Copper in Chile and Peru and iron ore in Brazil could each cover the gap alone, which says where any real diversion would have to happen: in the two or three commodities that carry the region's trade, not in lithium or rare earths.

What history says about shocks is weak but not silent [shocks]: after the Chinese export-control measures of 2023–2024 and the US tariff and strategy measures before them, the share of exports going to China rose on average by three to four points within two years. Those measures coincided with the pull of Chinese demand and did not reverse it. The event list is in draft and the windows overlap, so this is a direction, not an estimate.

Things to watch, each of which would show first in a layer this page tracks: whether the 2026 surge of statements, a third of the whole dataset, is followed by commitments in the DFC and EXIM record; whether the Section 232 copper tariff and the Chancay port move Chile's and Peru's shares in the 2026 trade data; whether Argentina's RIGI and Brazil's critical-minerals law bring the US-origin finance the statements promise; and whether the Chinese export controls of 2025 change the direction of niobium, graphite and rare-earth flows from Brazil.

## Bold readings, stated as such

- The United States is losing the mineral contest it talks about most, and the statements dataset records that talk, not a strategy with money behind it [who_talks_who_pays, attention].
- Chinese finance did not buy the minerals; prices and geology did. Dependence on China is a market outcome that the finance only accompanied [panel, money_without_trade].
- Hedging is rational and durable: no South American executive gains by choosing, and the data show none choosing [hedging, words_vs_trade_PER].
- Lithium and rare earths are political minerals; copper, iron ore, gold and silver are economic ones. Policy aimed at the first will not move the second [talk_vs_trade_CHL, talk_vs_trade_BRA, parity].
- The more democratic countries buy more of their mineral imports from the United States, but the data show no such association for what they sell. The US advantage in this region runs through what it sells, not what it buys [panel].

## What would change this reading

A validated text model that moved the legislative stances; a second coder on the statements that shifted the executives' scores; DFC or EXIM commitments after 2024 that approach the Chinese figures; a 2026 trade year in which Chile's or Peru's share to the United States rose by more than the scenario's two points; AidData's next release covering 2022–2024. Each would appear on this page before it changed the words here.
